name: HGH Fragment 176-191
lead: HGH Fragment 176-191 (also written hGH frag 176-191 or just "frag") is a synthetic peptide matching the final sixteen amino acids at the C-terminal end of the 191-residue human growth hormone (hGH) molecule. It is sold online as a research chemical and is discussed in bodybuilding and fat-loss forums as a way to get growth hormone's fat-mobilising action without its growth-promoting effects [1][2].

The appearance goal is a leaner physique: users aim to lose stubborn body fat during cutting phases so that muscle and facial definition show. Growth hormone promotes lipolysis (fat breakdown) and raises free fatty acid levels [13], and the idea behind the fragment is that this activity sits in the tail of the molecule.

The rationale rests largely on research on AOD9604, a modified version of the same segment, with a tyrosine replacing the N-terminal phenylalanine, that was developed as an anti-obesity candidate and tested in humans [11]. Wikipedia notes that the unmodified fragment has been presented as lipolytic by extrapolation from AOD9604 data and that, unlike AOD9604, it has not itself been studied in humans [1]. Published work on the exact peptide is mostly laboratory research, and it is not approved as a medicine [1][2].
In community discussion it appears in bodybuilding contest-prep logs alongside other peptides, stimulants and thyroid hormone, usually as an add-on for the final weeks before a show [3][4][5][9].

paras: Human growth hormone is a single-chain protein of 191 amino acids and about 22 kilodaltons, made by the anterior pituitary [13]. Fragment 176-191 reproduces its terminal segment. Wikipedia gives its sequence and notes a disulfide bridge between the two cysteine residues, which gives the peptide a loop shape [1]. A recent laboratory paper writes the sequence with a tyrosine at the start (YLRIVQCRSVEGSCGF), the form commonly sold, and describes the fragment as reported to enhance lipid breakdown in mice [14].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia whose content should be treated cautiously, says the peptide is made by solid-phase synthesis and purified by chromatography [2]. Suppliers are largely unregulated online sellers, and independent analyses of vial purity and identity have not been published.
Wikipedia's chemistry entry gives the formula C78H123N23O22S2, a molar mass of about 1,799 g/mol and a CAS number of 66004-57-7 [1].

The proposed rationale is that the C-terminal region of growth hormone carries the hormone's lipolytic (fat-breakdown) activity, so a fragment could stimulate fat metabolism without the receptor-mediated effects that raise IGF-1 and impair glucose handling.[2] Descriptions of this mechanism rest mainly on rodent work and on studies of AOD9604, and the receptor pathway has not been clearly defined.[2][6]

A 2001 paper titled as a comparison of the effects of hGH and its lipolytic fragment AOD9604 on lipid metabolism, and a 2000 paper on oral administration of a synthetic hGH fragment, are the kind of animal studies cited in support of the lipolytic idea.[6][7]

Growth hormone was long known to mobilise fat and to raise blood glucose, and its use for performance and anti-aging spread as recombinant hormone replaced cadaver-derived hormone after 1985 [13]. Athletes have used hGH since at least 1982, and the IOC and NCAA ban it [13]. Researchers who looked for which part of the molecule carried the fat-breakdown activity reported lipolytic effects for C-terminal fragments in rodents around 2000 and 2001 [6][7].

Wikipedia's article on the fragment gives no account of its commercial origins; the best-documented line of development is AOD9604, the modified analogue, whose clinical programme ended in 2007 according to Wikipedia [11]. The unmodified peptide entered bodybuilding forums by 2008 as a research chemical and was discussed there as a cutting aid [5].

AOD9604 is a 16-amino-acid fragment of human growth hormone covering residues 176 to 191 in which a tyrosine replaces the N-terminal phenylalanine; it was designed to keep fat-breakdown activity without the growth effects of the full hormone [11]. In mice it appears to raise fat breakdown by upregulating beta-3 adrenergic receptors, and mice lacking those receptors did not respond [11].

Wikipedia reports that early human trials showed lipolytic activity without raised IGF-1, that a 12-week randomised trial found people on AOD9604 lost on average 1.8 kg more than those on placebo, and that development was halted after poor efficacy in a later 24-week trial; it dates the end of development to 2007 based on 2013 citations [11]. Because the product sold online is the unmodified fragment, these findings are not direct data on it [1][11].
No studies found of HGH Fragment 176-191 itself in humans. Wikipedia states that, in contrast to AOD9604, the unmodified fragment has not been studied in humans.[1]

Related research: AOD9604, the modified analogue, has been tested in human trials, and Wikipedia describes the fat-loss claims for the unmodified fragment as extrapolated from that data [1]. A 2022 study by Habibullah and colleagues combined molecular docking with cell culture, using the fragment in doxorubicin-loaded chitosan nanoparticles; the peptide-containing formulation had an IC50 of about 1.5 micrograms per millilitre against MCF-7 breast cancer cells versus 1.85 for free doxorubicin, and the authors noted the work was in a single cell line [8][14]. This concerned drug delivery and not fat loss. No registered clinical trial of the exact peptide was found.

The AOD9604 programme gives the nearest human data: Wikipedia reports early human trials showed lipolytic activity without raised IGF-1, a 12-week randomised trial in which participants on AOD9604 lost on average 1.8 kg more than those on placebo, and the halting of development after poor efficacy in a later 24-week trial [11]. In mice, AOD9604 appears to act through beta-3 adrenergic receptors, and mice lacking them did not respond [11].
A literature search of the exact peptide returns animal and laboratory work and cell-culture drug-delivery studies, which do not address its effect on body fat in people [8].

Because the exact peptide has not been studied in people, no human safety profile has been published. It is not approved by regulators for any medical use and is distributed as a research chemical.[1][2] Grokipedia states that studies of AOD9604 reported no effect on IGF-1 or glucose tolerance, but this concerns the modified analogue rather than the fragment sold online.[2]

Wikipedia notes that AOD9604 is banned in athletes and tested for in competition [11], and growth hormone is prohibited by the IOC and NCAA [13]; competitors in tested sports are therefore subject to anti-doping rules. Anti-doping bodies publish the current status of individual fragments.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, discussions from 2008 onward mention the fragment as an adjunct for fat loss during contest preparation, often together with GH secretagogues such as GHRP-6, CJC-1295 or sermorelin, and with clenbuterol, ECA stacks or T3.[3][4][5][9][10] Users share anecdotal logs, and some posts ask for advice on how to use it, which this article does not reproduce. Posters also note uncertainty about whether physicians would prescribe it.[4]
Reports in these threads are self-reported and uncontrolled, and combine the fragment with other agents, so they do not isolate its effect.

The US Food and Drug Administration maintains a list of bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks when used in compounding. It lists AOD-9604, saying that compounded versions may pose significant risk for immunogenicity for certain routes and noting serious adverse events that may be associated with it, though causality is unclear [12]. The same FDA page lists CJC-1295, ipamorelin, GHRP-2 and GHRP-6, peptides that appear in the same forum threads as the fragment, citing immunogenicity concerns and, for some, serious adverse events [12]. The FDA page does not list the unmodified fragment 176-191 by name.

lore.intro: Bodybuilding forums such as T Nation present the fragment as a fat-loss peptide used in cutting phases, usually alongside other agents.[3][5]

claims.claim: Frag 176-191 is the part of growth hormone that burns fat, without the other GH effects
claims.believers: Forum posters describe the fragment as the chain of growth hormone responsible for fat loss and use it in results logs and contest preparation.[3][9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the lipolytic reputation was extrapolated from data on AOD9604 and that the unmodified fragment has not been studied in humans.[1]

claims.claim: Stacking it with GH secretagogues, clenbuterol or T3 improves fat loss
claims.believers: Contest-prep posters report combining the fragment with GHRP-6, CJC-1295, clenbuterol or T3 in the final weeks before a show.[4][5][10]
claims.experts: No published study has tested such combinations; reports are anecdotal and confounded by simultaneous agents.

claims.claim: It is safe because it does not raise IGF-1 or blood sugar
claims.believers: Proponents argue the fragment lacks the growth-promoting actions of full-length hGH.[2]
claims.experts: Data on lack of IGF-1 effect come from studies of the modified analogue AOD9604, and no human safety data exist for the unmodified peptide sold online.[1][2]

claims.claim: Frag can be run in a daily protocol alongside clenbuterol or ECA for cutting
claims.believers: A 2008 T Nation poster described pairing the fragment with clenbuterol and an ECA stack in a prep-style schedule, reporting having obtained high-purity material [5].
claims.experts: No published study has examined such combinations, and the unmodified fragment has no human trial data; regulators do not approve it for any use [1].

claims.claim: The fragment is not a growth-hormone analogue that builds muscle, only a fat-loss tool
claims.believers: Posters describe it as the chain of growth hormone responsible for weight loss and contrast it with full-length GH [3].
claims.experts: Growth hormone itself raises lipolysis and affects glucose [13]; Wikipedia says the fragment's lipolytic reputation is extrapolated from AOD9604 [1].

claims.claim: Doctors may prescribe frag as part of a peptide protocol
claims.believers: A T Nation poster suggests looking at frag 176-191 for fat burning but is unsure a doctor will prescribe it [4].
claims.experts: The FDA lists related AOD-9604, CJC-1295 and GHRP peptides among bulk substances flagged for safety risks in compounding [12].

angle.text: People in bodybuilding circles use the fragment as a cutting-phase add-on, aiming to lose stubborn body fat so muscle and facial definition show. The fat-loss effect is the claim made for it; it has been proposed by extrapolation from data on the related peptide AOD9604.
